XOM.what: The largest US oil company. It pumps oil and gas around the world, refines it into fuels, and makes chemicals and plastics.
XOM.money: Selling oil, gas, fuel and chemicals. Profits rise and fall with oil prices, but its refineries and chemical plants soften the swings.
XOM.watch: Oil prices and how much it pays back to shareholders through dividends and buybacks.

CVX.what: The second largest US oil company. It drills for oil and gas, refines fuel, and sells it at Chevron and Texaco stations.
CVX.money: Selling oil, gas and refined fuels. Its recent purchase of Hess added a large stake in fast-growing oil fields off Guyana.
CVX.watch: Oil prices and how smoothly the Hess oil fields grow.

COP.what: The biggest US company that only finds and pumps oil and gas, with no refineries or gas stations.
COP.money: Selling raw oil and gas. With no refining business, its profits follow oil prices closely.
COP.watch: Oil prices and its costs per barrel.

EOG.what: A US oil and gas driller known for low costs, working mainly in Texas, New Mexico and Ohio.
EOG.money: Selling oil and gas from its own wells.
EOG.watch: Oil prices and whether it keeps costs low as older wells decline.

OXY.what: An oil and gas producer focused on the Permian Basin in Texas, with a chemicals business and a project to pull carbon dioxide out of the air.
OXY.money: Mostly selling oil and gas; its chemicals unit adds steadier income.
OXY.watch: Debt left over from past purchases and oil prices. Berkshire Hathaway is a major owner.

DVN.what: A US oil and gas producer working in Texas, Oklahoma, North Dakota and Wyoming.
DVN.money: Selling oil and gas. It pays a dividend that moves up and down with profits.
DVN.watch: Oil prices and the size of its variable dividend.

FANG.what: A Texas oil driller that works only in the Permian Basin, the most productive US oil region.
FANG.money: Selling oil and gas from its wells.
FANG.watch: Oil prices and how well it combines the Endeavor business it bought.

EQT.what: The largest natural gas producer in the US, drilling in Pennsylvania and West Virginia. It also owns pipelines.
EQT.money: Selling natural gas, so its profits follow US gas prices.
EQT.watch: Natural gas prices, which depend on weather, exports and demand from data centers.

EXE.what: A large US natural gas producer formed when Chesapeake Energy merged with Southwestern Energy.
EXE.money: Selling natural gas from Louisiana, Pennsylvania and West Virginia.
EXE.watch: Natural gas prices and new demand from gas export terminals.

LNG.what: The largest US exporter of liquefied natural gas. It cools gas into a liquid and ships it overseas.
LNG.money: Mostly long contracts, often 15 to 20 years, where buyers pay fixed fees whether or not they take the gas.
LNG.watch: World gas prices and the timing of new export capacity.

VG.what: A newer US exporter of liquefied natural gas with large plants in Louisiana.
VG.money: Long contracts with overseas buyers plus selling some cargoes at market prices.
VG.watch: Debt from building plants and disputes with past customers over delayed cargoes.

KMI.what: One of the largest pipeline operators in North America, moving natural gas, fuels and carbon dioxide.
KMI.money: Fees for moving and storing energy, which are steadier than oil and gas prices.
KMI.watch: Growth in gas demand from power plants and exports, and its debt.

WMB.what: A pipeline company whose Transco line carries much of the natural gas used on the US East Coast.
WMB.money: Fees for moving and processing natural gas.
WMB.watch: New pipeline projects and power plant demand for gas.

ET.what: A huge pipeline partnership moving oil, gas and fuels across the US.
ET.money: Fees for transporting, storing and processing energy. Owners receive large cash payouts.
ET.watch: Debt levels and tax paperwork: it sends a K-1 form, not a standard 1099.

EPD.what: A pipeline partnership focused on gas liquids, oil and petrochemicals along the Gulf Coast.
EPD.money: Fees for moving and processing energy, known for steady payouts that have risen for over 25 years.
EPD.watch: Export volumes and the K-1 tax form it sends owners.

OKE.what: A pipeline company moving natural gas and gas liquids, mostly in the middle of the US.
OKE.money: Fees for gathering, processing and moving gas and liquids.
OKE.watch: How well it combines its recent purchases and drilling activity on its pipelines.

NEE.what: The owner of Florida Power and Light and the world's largest builder of wind and solar farms.
NEE.money: Regulated electricity bills in Florida plus selling clean power under long contracts.
NEE.watch: Interest rates, clean energy tax credits and demand from data centers.

SO.what: A power company serving Georgia, Alabama and Mississippi, and owner of the newest US nuclear reactors at Plant Vogtle.
SO.money: Regulated electricity and gas bills, with rates approved by state regulators.
SO.watch: Rate decisions in Georgia and data center growth in its area.

DUK.what: One of the largest US power companies, serving the Carolinas, Florida, Indiana, Ohio and Kentucky.
DUK.watch: Its large building plan, which needs new debt, and state rate approvals.

AEP.what: A power company that owns the largest high-voltage transmission network in the US, serving 11 states.
AEP.money: Regulated electricity bills and fees for moving power over its lines.
AEP.watch: Data center demand in Ohio and Texas and the cost of building lines.

D.what: A power company serving Virginia and the Carolinas, home to the largest cluster of data centers in the world.
D.watch: Its large offshore wind farm and data center demand in northern Virginia.

SRE.what: An energy company owning San Diego Gas and Electric and Southern California Gas, plus a large stake in Oncor, the biggest power line company in Texas.
SRE.money: Regulated bills in California and Texas plus a gas export business.
SRE.watch: Wildfire risk in California and growth in Texas.

ETR.what: A power company serving Louisiana, Arkansas, Mississippi and Texas, with a large fleet of nuclear plants.
ETR.money: Regulated electricity bills, with growing sales to factories and data centers.
ETR.watch: Hurricane damage and new industrial customers along the Gulf Coast.

XEL.what: A power company serving eight states in the Midwest and West, and a leader in wind power.
XEL.watch: Wildfire lawsuits in Colorado and Texas and its clean energy building plan.

NGG.what: A British company that runs power lines in England and Wales and power and gas networks in New York and Massachusetts.
NGG.money: Regulated fees for carrying electricity and gas, set by regulators in the UK and US.
NGG.watch: Its large upgrade plan for the UK grid and the currency exchange rate.

CEG.what: The largest owner of nuclear power plants in the US, and the biggest producer of clean electricity.
CEG.money: Selling electricity at market prices and under long contracts, including deals with tech companies such as Microsoft and Meta.
CEG.watch: Power prices, data center deals and how it combines Calpine, which it bought.

VST.what: A Texas-based power producer with nuclear, gas and coal plants, and a large retail electricity business.
VST.money: Selling electricity to the grid and directly to homes and businesses.
VST.watch: Power prices in Texas and new deals with data centers.

NRG.what: A power producer and retail electricity seller in Texas and the Northeast, which also owns Vivint home security.
NRG.money: Selling electricity and home services to millions of customers.
NRG.watch: Power prices and new gas plants it is building for data center demand.

TLN.what: A power producer that owns the Susquehanna nuclear plant in Pennsylvania, which supplies an Amazon data center.
TLN.money: Selling electricity at market prices and under a long contract with Amazon.
TLN.watch: Power prices in the Mid-Atlantic and more data center deals.

BEP.what: One of the world's largest owners of hydro, wind and solar power plants, run by Brookfield.
BEP.money: Selling clean power under long contracts, often linked to inflation.
BEP.watch: Interest rates and new corporate deals, such as its Microsoft agreement.

CCJ.what: A Canadian company and one of the world's largest uranium miners. It also owns 49% of Westinghouse, which designs nuclear reactors.
CCJ.money: Selling uranium to power plants, mostly under long contracts, plus fuel services and reactor work.
CCJ.watch: Uranium prices and new reactor orders for Westinghouse.

LEU.what: A US company that enriches uranium, the step that turns mined uranium into fuel reactors can use.
LEU.money: Selling enrichment services to utilities and running a government project for advanced reactor fuel.
LEU.watch: Limits on Russian uranium imports and US funding for new enrichment plants.

BWXT.what: The builder of nuclear reactors for US Navy submarines and aircraft carriers, also making medical isotopes and parts for power plants.
BWXT.money: Mostly long government contracts, which are very steady.
BWXT.watch: Navy shipbuilding budgets and new work on small reactors.

UEC.what: A US uranium miner with projects in Texas, Wyoming and Canada.
UEC.money: Selling uranium, though production is still small and profits are uneven.
UEC.watch: Uranium prices and how quickly its mines ramp up.

NXE.what: A Canadian company developing one of the world's largest untapped uranium deposits, in Saskatchewan.
NXE.money: Nothing yet. It is building its first mine and has no sales.
NXE.watch: Government approvals and the cost of building the mine.

GEV.what: The former energy arm of General Electric, making gas turbines, wind turbines and power grid equipment.
GEV.money: Selling and servicing power equipment. Gas turbines are sold out years ahead because of data center demand.
GEV.watch: Its order backlog and whether its wind business stops losing money.

VRT.what: A maker of the power and cooling equipment that keeps data centers running.
VRT.money: Selling and servicing equipment to data centers, with strong demand from artificial intelligence buildouts.
VRT.watch: Spending on data centers by the big tech companies.

ETN.what: A large industrial company making electrical equipment such as switchgear, breakers and power systems.
ETN.money: Selling electrical gear to data centers, utilities, factories and buildings.
ETN.watch: Data center and factory building and its growing order backlog.

PWR.what: The largest US contractor that builds and repairs power lines, substations and pipelines.
PWR.money: Getting paid by utilities and companies to build energy projects.
PWR.watch: Utility building budgets and the shortage of skilled workers.

HUBB.what: A maker of electrical parts for power grids and buildings, such as connectors, pole hardware and wiring devices.
HUBB.money: Selling parts to utilities and contractors.

POWL.what: A Houston company that builds custom electrical equipment for oil and gas plants, utilities and data centers.
POWL.money: Selling large, engineered electrical systems on project orders.
POWL.watch: New orders and how much of its business comes from data centers.

ITRI.what: A maker of smart meters and software that help utilities measure and manage electricity, gas and water use.
ITRI.money: Selling meters and charging utilities for software and network services.
ITRI.watch: Utility spending on grid upgrades and growth in its software business.

FSLR.what: The largest US maker of solar panels, using its own thin-film technology that does not depend on Chinese supply chains.
FSLR.money: Selling panels to developers of large solar farms, helped by US manufacturing tax credits.
FSLR.watch: Changes to clean energy tax credits and tariffs on imported panels.

ENPH.what: A maker of the small electronic devices that convert power from home solar panels, plus home batteries.
ENPH.money: Selling equipment through installers to homeowners.
ENPH.watch: Home solar demand, interest rates and the end of tax credits for homeowners.

NXT.what: The leading maker of solar trackers, the motorized frames that turn panels to follow the sun.
NXT.money: Selling trackers and software to builders of large solar farms.
NXT.watch: Large solar farm demand and US tax credit rules.

SEDG.what: A maker of electronics that manage and convert power from rooftop solar panels.
SEDG.money: Selling equipment to installers, mostly in the US and Europe.
SEDG.watch: Whether it returns to profit after a sharp sales drop.

ARRY.what: A maker of solar trackers for large solar farms.
ARRY.money: Selling trackers to solar farm builders.
ARRY.watch: Competition with Nextracker and solar project timing.

RUN.what: The largest US home solar company, which installs panels and batteries and often leases them to homeowners.
RUN.money: Monthly payments from homeowners over 20 to 25 years, plus selling tax credits.
RUN.watch: Interest rates, its heavy debt and changes to home solar tax credits.

FLNC.what: A maker of large battery systems that store power for utilities and the grid, backed by Siemens and AES.
FLNC.money: Selling and servicing battery storage projects.
FLNC.watch: Battery costs, tariffs on Chinese parts and project delays.

OKLO.what: A startup designing small nuclear reactors that can power data centers and towns.
OKLO.money: Nothing yet. It has no sales and is waiting for permission from nuclear regulators to build.
OKLO.watch: Approval from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission and signed customer deals.

SMR.what: The first company with a small modular nuclear reactor design approved by US regulators.
SMR.money: Very little so far, mostly engineering work. It needs a customer to order and build a plant.
SMR.watch: A first firm order. Its main owner, Fluor, has been selling shares.

XE.what: A developer of small, high-temperature nuclear reactors and the special fuel they use, backed by Amazon and Dow.
XE.money: Mostly government funding and engineering work for now.
XE.watch: Progress on its first plant in Texas and fuel factory in Tennessee.

STDN.what: A company making the tiny coated-particle nuclear fuel (called TRISO) that many advanced reactor designs use.
STDN.money: Early fuel contracts with reactor developers and the government.
STDN.watch: Whether advanced reactors get built, since they are its future customers.

FRVO.what: A company drilling deep geothermal wells to make steady, clean power from underground heat, using oil and gas drilling methods.
FRVO.money: Selling power under long contracts to utilities and tech companies such as Google.
FRVO.watch: Its first large plant in Utah coming online on time and on budget.

NNE.what: A startup designing very small portable nuclear reactors.
NNE.money: Nothing yet. It has no sales and is years from a working reactor.
NNE.watch: Regulatory progress and how much cash it raises by selling new shares.

EOSE.what: A maker of zinc-based batteries that store power for the grid without using lithium.
EOSE.money: Selling battery systems, but it still loses money on each unit as it scales up.
EOSE.watch: Whether its factory reaches lower costs and the steady cash it needs from loans.
